tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

level.description: Effort level the review ran at

file.description: Repo-relative path of the file the finding is in

short_summary.description: Compressed label for compact UI (≤60 chars): the claim alone, no rationale or consequence clause

category.description: Short kebab-case slug of the finding type, e.g. "correctness", "simplification", "efficiency", "test-coverage"

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

Do not choose one silently. for (const delta of [-120, -90, -60, -30, 30, 60, 90, 120]) { const alternate = new Date(result.getTime() + delta * 60_000); if (alternate.getFullYear() === date.getFullYear() && alternate.getMonth() === date.getMonth() && alternate.getDate() === date.getDate() && alternate.getHours() === hour && alternate.getMinutes() === minute) return null; } return result; } function option(id: string, label: string, date: Date, prefs: ReminderPreferences, now: Date): ReminderTimeOption { const at = localDate(date, prefs.hour, prefs.minute); return { id, label: at && at.getTime() > now.getTime() ? label : `${label} (unavailable)`, dueAt: at && at.getTime() > now.getTime() ? at.toISOString() : null }; } export function getReminderPresets(now: Date, preferences: ReminderPreferences): ReminderTimeOption[] { const tomorrow = new Date(now.getFullYear(), now.getMonth(), now.getDate() + 1); const daysUntilMonday = (8 - now.getDay()) % 7 || 7; const monday = new Date(now.getFullYear(), now.getMonth(), now.getDate() + daysUntilMonday); const daysUntilSaturday = (6 - now.getDay() + 7) % 7 || 7; const saturday = new Date(now.getFullYear(), now.getMonth(), now.getDate() + daysUntilSaturday); const suggestions = [option('tomorrow', 'Tomorrow', tomorrow, preferences, now), option('next-week', 'Next Monday', monday, preferences, now), option('next-weekend', 'Next weekend', saturday, preferences, now)]; // On Sunday, Tomorrow and Next Monday can be the same available instant. // Keep the explicit weekday choice and retain unavailable options. const tomorrowOption = suggestions[0]!; const mondayOption = suggestions[1]!; const distinctSuggestions = tomorrowOption.dueAt && tomorrowOption.dueAt === mondayOption.dueAt ? suggestions.filter(suggestion => suggestion.id !== 'tomorrow') : suggestions; return [...distinctSuggestions, { id: 'someday', label: 'Someday', dueAt: null }]; } function readable(date: Date): string { return new Intl.DateTimeFormat(undefined, { dateStyle: 'medium', timeStyle: 'short' }).format(date); } export function parseReminderTime(input: string, now: Date, preferences: ReminderPreferences): ReminderTimeResult { const text = input.trim().toLowerCase(); if (text === 'someday') return { ok: true, dueAt: null, label: 'Someday' }; const iso = input.trim(); if (/^\d{4}-\d\d-\d\dT\d\d:\d\d(?::\d\d(?:\.\d+)?)?(?:Z|[+-]\d\d:\d\d)$/i.test(iso)) { const date = new Date(iso); const calendar = iso.match(/^(\d{4})-(\d\d)-(\d\d)T/i)!; const calendarCheck = new Date(`${calendar[1]}-${calendar[2]}-${calendar[3]}T00:00:00Z`); if (!Number.isFinite(date.getTime()) || calendarCheck.toISOString().slice(0, 10) !== iso.slice(0, 10)) return { ok: false, error: 'Enter a valid date and time.' }; if (date <= now) return { ok: false, error: 'Choose a time in the future.' }; return { ok: true, dueAt: iso.endsWith('Z') ? date.toISOString() : iso, label: readable(date) }; } let target: Date | null = null; let label = ''; const base = new Date(now.getFullYear(), now.getMonth(), now.getDate()); const clockTime = text.match(/^(\d{1,2})(?::(\d{2}))?\s*(am|pm)$/); const relative = text.match(/^(\d+)\s+days?$/); if (relative) { const count = Number(relative[1]); if (count < 1 || count > 36500) return { ok: false, error: 'Enter a number of days from 1 to 36500.' }; target = new Date(base.getFullYear(), base.getMonth(), base.getDate() + count); label = `${count} day${count === 1 ? '' : 's'}`; } else if (text === 'tomorrow') { target = new Date(base.getFullYear(), base.getMonth(), base.getDate() + 1); label = 'Tomorrow'; } else if (text === 'next monday' || text === 'next week') { const add = (8 - now.getDay()) % 7 || 7; target = new Date(base.getFullYear(), base.getMonth(), base.getDate() + add); label = 'Next Monday'; } else if (text === 'next weekend') { const add = (6 - now.getDay() + 7) % 7 || 7; target = new Date(base.getFullYear(), base.getMonth(), base.getDate() + add); label = 'Next weekend'; } else if (clockTime) { const clockHour = Number(clockTime[1]); const clockMinute = Number(clockTime[2] ?? 0); if (clockHour < 1 || clockHour > 12 || clockMinute > 59) return { ok: false, error: 'Enter a valid clock time, such as “9:30 am”.' }; const hour = clockHour % 12 + (clockTime[3] === 'pm' ? 12 : 0); target = new Date(base); label = `${clockHour}:${String(clockMinute).padStart(2, '0')} ${clockTime[3]!.toUpperCase()}`; let at = localDate(target, hour, clockMinute); content.text:
I found three P2 issues and no P0 or P1 issues. I reproduced all three with a scratch vitest probe in jsdom, using the browser fake only as a UI harness, so none of this says anything about native persistence. I didn't edit any repo files.

**P2 — Escape from a new picker leaves keyboard triage stuck on the header button**
- **Where:** `/home/exedev/.t3/worktrees/email-os/t3-0ce43878/src/App.vue:598-602` (`reminderDismissed` calls `closeDrawer()`), which then runs `closeDrawer` at `src/App.vue:609`: `drawerToggles.get(closing)?.focus()`.
- **What happens:** before this diff, dismissing the picker kept the drawer open. Now it closes the drawer, and `closeDrawer` focuses the drawer's registered toggle, which is the header "Reminders (G then H)" button (`App.vue:2281`).
- **Repro:** focus an Inbox row, press H, then press Escape. `document.activeElement` ends up as the button titled "Reminders (G then H)".
- **Impact:** with a button focused, `actionShortcutBlocked` / `buttonOwns` (`App.vue:1841-1860`, `1976`) blocks H, E, S and Z, and J/K list navigation (`browsingOwns` requires `!buttonOwns`). After cancelling a reminder, the keyboard user has to click or Tab back into the list. The same happens when the picker was opened from a row's clock button. The existing test (`tests/reminders.component.test.ts:253-258`) only checks that the panel is gone, not where focus goes.
- **Fix:** in `reminderDismissed`, set `drawer.value = null` and restore the origin directly: `focusFocusedRow()` for the list, the reader focus when the reader was open, or the row's remind button. Don't route through `closeDrawer()`. Add a focus assertion to the test.

**P2 — Escape or a backdrop click while a save is in flight drops the acknowledgement and the recovery controls**
- **Where:**
  - `src/components/ReminderPicker.vue:84` (`onDialogKeydown`) and the template backdrop `@click.self="emit('dismiss')"`: neither checks `props.disabled`.
  - `src/components/RemindersPanel.vue:110-117`: `clearPicker` bumps `editorGeneration` and clears `busy` and `retry`.
  - `src/App.vue:1932-1937`: the global Escape handler closes the drawer.
- **Repro:** H → choose Someday → click "Schedule reminder" with `put` still pending. The input becomes disabled and focus falls to BODY. Press Escape: the panel unmounts. When `put` resolves, no `reminder-confirmation` appears. Pressing Escape inside the dialog, or clicking the backdrop, takes the same path through `dismissPicker`.
- **Impact:**
  - The backend may already have committed the reminder, so the conversation is hidden from Inbox with no confirmation, and the `mailbox.refresh()` in `reminderScheduled` never runs.
  - If the request actually fails or the acknowledgement is lost, "Retry exact request" and the error are discarded silently. This contradicts the documented rule (`docs/ux-11-local-reminders.md`): "Failures retain their recovery controls…"
  - The focus trap also stops working while focus is on BODY.
- **Fix:**
  - While `busy`, ignore dismiss in the picker (Escape and backdrop) and suppress the App drawer Escape.
  - Move focus to the dialog container or the live region before disabling the controls, so focus doesn't fall to BODY.
  - Alternatively, let an in-flight `put` finish and emit `scheduled` even after the editor is dismissed.

**P2 — Typing "next week" and pressing Enter schedules Saturday, not Monday**
- **Where:** `src/components/ReminderPicker.vue:24` (the `options` filter matches by substring) and line 63 (`options.value.find(selectable)` is auto-chosen before parsing).
- **Repro:** typing `next week` + Enter emits `2026-11-14T08:00:00.000Z` (Next weekend, a Saturday). `parseReminderTime('next week')` returns Next Monday, `2026-11-09`, because `reminder-time.ts:63` deliberately treats "next week" as Next Monday.
- **Impact:** a supported phrase resolves to a different day than the parser defines. The resolved time is shown before saving, but the user has to notice the mismatch.
- **Fix:** run `parseReminderTime` first on unhighlighted Enter, or only auto-pick a suggestion on an exact or prefix match that the parser rejects.

**P2 — The picker accepts ISO times that the native store rejects, and the error message is misleading**
- **Where:** `src/lib/reminder-time.ts:52-58`. The regex makes seconds optional and allows fractional seconds, and a value with an offset is returned unchanged.
- **Repro:**
  - `2030-11-03T09:00-05:00` is accepted with `dueAt` `2030-11-03T09:00-05:00`.
  - `2030-11-03T09:00:00.5Z` is accepted as `…09:00:00.500Z`.
- **Why native rejects them:** `crates/mail-core/src/gmail/store.rs:919-933` uses chrono `parse_from_rfc3339`, which requires seconds, and it also rejects any non-zero fraction (`timestamp_subsec_nanos() != 0`). The fixture store (`crates/mail-core/src/store/reminders.rs:125`) uses the same parser. The browser fake regex also requires seconds.
- **Impact:** the picker shows "Selected …" and enables "Schedule reminder", then the save fails with `RemindersPanel.vue:59` ("…must include Z or a numeric timezone offset."). That message is wrong, because the value does include an offset.
- **Fix:** make seconds mandatory and reject fractions in the parser, or normalise by adding `:00` when seconds are missing. Add parser tests for both cases.

**Validation:**
- I didn't run the full suites, the Rust or native checks, or any rendered browser, VoiceOver or NVDA tests, so none of those results should be inferred from this review.
- The probe test and its config are in `/tmp/claude-1000/-home-exedev--t3-worktrees-email-os-t3-0ce43878/7fe75ce7-ca94-4d50-97d4-b1831b39e827/scratchpad/probe.test.ts` and `/tmp/claude-1000/-home-exedev--t3-worktrees-email-os-t3-0ce43878/7fe75ce7-ca94-4d50-97d4-b1831b39e827/scratchpad/vitest.probe.config.ts`.
- What I traced without finding a defect: DST fold and gap rejection, the Sunday duplicate-suggestion removal, untouched reschedule saving the exact value, the account and epoch guards in `reminderScheduled`, the navigation-precedence token, the receipt-based confirmation copy, and the timer cleanup on unmount.

Merge verdict: OK with notes
